lines.text: A land shaped by a great river, by empires and by faith. This is the story of Pakistan, from the first farmers of the Indus to today.
Long before people, the Indus River began to carve its way from Tibet to the sea. Everything in this story depends on its water.
At Mehrgarh, in Balochistan, people were farming nine thousand years ago, in one of the earliest villages of South Asia.
Along the river grew the Indus Valley Civilisation, with planned cities, drains and standard weights, and a script nobody has read.
Its greatest city was Mohenjo-daro, in Sindh, with straight streets and brick houses laid out with remarkable care.
Near today's Islamabad, Taxila grew into a city of learning that would draw students for more than a thousand years.
The land around it, Gandhara, became famous for Buddhist art that blended Greek and Indian styles.
By about the year one thousand, Lahore was rising, a city that would later be a Mughal capital of forts, gardens and mosques.
There the emperor Aurangzeb built the Badshahi Mosque in red sandstone, one of the great mosques of the world.
On the coast, the town of Karachi was founded, and grew into Pakistan's largest city and port.
Under British rule, a lawyer named Muhammad Ali Jinnah came to lead the Muslim League, and would become the founder of Pakistan.
The poet and philosopher Muhammad Iqbal was the first to call for a Muslim state in the north-west of India.
General Zia-ul-Haq would one day seize power and rule for eleven years, until his death in a plane crash.
Zulfikar Ali Bhutto would become prime minister, only to be overthrown by that general and hanged.
In 1940, the Muslim League met in Lahore and called for independent Muslim states. The idea of Pakistan had become a demand.
Seven years later it came true. In August 1947, Pakistan was born as a homeland for the Muslims of British India.
But partition came at a terrible price. Millions crossed the new borders in both directions, and violence killed a great many.
Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan would carry qawwali, the devotional music of the Sufis, to audiences around the world.
Shehbaz Sharif would become prime minister in 2022.
Imran Khan would captain Pakistan at cricket, become prime minister, and later be sent to jail.
Benazir Bhutto, daughter of Zulfikar, would become the first woman to lead a modern Muslim-majority country, before her assassination in 2007.
In 1954, climbers first reached the top of K2, the second-highest mountain on Earth, on Pakistan's border with China.
In the sixties, a new planned capital, Islamabad, was built below the Margalla Hills.
In 1971 war with India ended in surrender at Dhaka. The eastern half of the country broke away and became Bangladesh.
In 1992 came a moment of joy, when Imran Khan's team won the Cricket World Cup.
Malala Yousafzai, shot by the Taliban for going to school, survived to become the youngest winner of the Nobel Peace Prize.
In May 1998, days after India, Pakistan tested its own nuclear weapons.
In October 2005, an earthquake in Kashmir killed some eighty thousand people.
In 2011, American forces found and killed Osama bin Laden in the town of Abbottabad.
In 2022, floods put a third of the country under water.
And in May 2025, after an attack in Kashmir, India and Pakistan traded missile and drone strikes in a brief, tense conflict.
From the cities of the Indus to a nation of millions, Pakistan's story still flows on.
